title: What Reflective Teaching Actually Means
brief: Define reflective teaching using the module's own language: thinking about what happens in the classroom both in terms of the teaching itself and in terms of the learner response, and then trying to improve it. Explain the four core self-questions the module provides (Were goals met? What worked? Did learners act as expected? How can sessions be improved?). Connect this to the module's description of good teachers as lifelong learners who learn from students, trial and error, peers, mentors, and academic information throughout their careers. Do not introduce research claims or external frameworks.

title: The Teacher Diary: A Practical Reflection Routine
brief: Explain the teacher diary as the module describes it: a journal in which, after each lesson, the teacher notes what happened, their own reactions and feelings, and the reactions they observed in students, and begins to pose questions about what they observed. Emphasize the module's point that diary writing requires discipline and regularity but need not be lengthy. Walk through the four categories of diary questions from the module (Lesson Objectives, Activities and Materials, Classroom Management, Overall), giving concrete examples of the questions listed under each. Include the module's creative prompt asking teachers to find a metaphor or image that captures the essence of the lesson.

title: Recordings, Portfolios, and Other Reflection Tools
brief: Draw on the module's Summary Discussion answer key for Module 14, which lists additional reflective practices beyond the diary: video or audio recordings of lessons with follow-up analysis, teaching portfolios, mentoring partnerships between new and more experienced teachers, and classroom assessment techniques in which teachers gather feedback (including anonymous feedback) from students to help shape curriculum and lessons. For each tool, use only the description the module provides. Note the module's point that reflective practice is also an integral part of formative peer observation, creating a bridge to the next section. Do not add detail beyond what the module supplies.

title: Peer Observation as Colleague, Not Evaluator
brief: Distinguish clearly between the module's two forms of observation: summative (evaluation for job retention, promotion, salary) and formative (helping teachers become better professionals). Explain the advantages the module names for peer observation specifically: observers are familiar with the teaching situation and its limitations, teachers can try to improve without fear of recorded evaluation, and a strong supportive atmosphere among faculty can develop. Address the module's named risks—bias from personal belief systems and personal relationships—and the module's remedy: training teachers well in the process. Use the module's vocabulary definition of 'formative observation' and 'peer observation' to anchor the explanation.

title: The Three-Step Peer Observation Process
brief: Walk through the module's three-step structure in practical terms: the pre-observation meeting (using the module's Pre-observation Discussion Guide questions to establish context and agree on a focus, with the module's emphasis that the observed teacher must have an important voice in deciding the focus), the observation itself (drawing on the module's description of the observer sitting quietly, taking notes, not interrupting, and the teacher teaching a normal class rather than a 'show' class), and the post-observation debriefing (using the module's Post-Observation Discussion Guide: asking how the lesson felt, reconfirming focus points, offering positive comments, making tactfully worded suggestions limited to the agreed focus, and ending courteously). Include the module's guidance that suggestions should be limited in number and that positive comments should be at least as numerous as suggestions for improvement.

title: Turning Reflection into One Concrete Change
brief: Draw on the module's Action Plan steps for both modules to show how reflection leads to a single, manageable next action rather than wholesale overhaul. Use the module's description of Teacher #1 in the video answer key—making small, incremental changes that are deliberate and purposeful—as the model. Incorporate the module's Peer Observation Guide reminder that a second observation can be planned to follow up on any changes the teacher wants to implement. Use the module's post-observation reflection questions ('What will I do the same next time? What will I do differently? Is there other information I need?') as the closing loop. Emphasize the module's point that the process is ongoing and that checking in with colleagues to exchange ideas and make adaptations is built into the cycle.
